components.text: Whether Paul's received formula supplies early, historically usable evidence for the claimed resurrection.
Whether quoting a received early proclamation is sufficient to warrant a historical conclusion about the reported event.
Whether an early resurrection report warrants inferring that the extraordinary event actually occurred.
Whether plurality of ancient appearance reports materially distinguishes them from religious narrative formation.
Whether numerous ancient appearance reports distinguish bodily resurrection from religious narrative under ordinary historical comparison.
Whether an early received report overcomes the absence of comparable credible present experience.
Whether ancient pagan narratives provide chronologically prior resurrection parallels relevant to the Christian claim.
Whether ancient dying-and-rising narratives supply relevant pre-Christian comparison for the Christian resurrection claim.
Whether the absence of an early Attis resurrection leaves the pagan-parallel case without a relevant analogue.
Whether the relevant Attis resurrection interpretation occurs only after Christianity and therefore lacks chronological priority.
Whether sufficiently early evidence exists for pagan dying-and-rising narratives relevant to comparison.
Whether the claimed Attis resurrection interpretation lacks pre-Christian documentary support.
Whether early Christian imitation or counterfeit explanations establish prior pagan resurrection parallels.
Whether pagan stories had a resurrection ending sufficiently like Christ's to establish the claimed parallel.
Whether an early Christian counterfeit explanation concedes chronologically prior pagan resurrection parallels.
Whether broad similarities establish a resurrection parallel with the same relevant ending.
Whether First Corinthians 15 supplies a coherent received tradition with historically identifiable human transmission.
Whether Paul's received First Corinthians tradition coheres with his claim to receive the gospel from no mortal source.
Whether Paul's claims of receiving from Christ and receiving delivered resurrection material are contradictory.
Whether Paul contradicts himself by describing gospel content as both received from Christ and delivered to him.
Whether the named writings and attributed teachers reliably establish an apostolic transmission chain.
Whether Gospel attributions and independence are sufficiently secure for multiple historical attestation.
Whether attributed New Testament and patristic writings reliably establish named apostolic authorship and transmission links.
Whether anonymous Gospel reports can be treated as identified and independent historical attestations.
Whether Paul's glorious and spiritual body language requires tangible physical continuity rather than spiritual existence.
Whether Paul's glorious or spiritual body language requires continuity with tangible flesh rather than a spiritual condition.
Whether Paul's spiritual-body language excludes an incorruptible but embodied resurrection condition.
Whether spiritual body in Paul means immaterial existence and conflicts with a flesh-and-bones resurrection depiction.
Whether Pauline usage is internally coherent across relevant passages.
Whether broader Pauline usage establishes that spiritual body remains tangibly continuous with mortal flesh.
Whether broader Pauline lexical usage establishes a tangible transformed body despite the immediate flesh-and-spirit contrast.
Whether disputed attribution and anonymous writings undermine the claimed apostolic pedigree of later agreement.
Whether geographically dispersed agreement can establish apostolic transmission despite disputed authorship and attribution.
Whether shared bodily belief resolves Paul's immediate lexical context.
Whether claimed apostolic succession uniquely explains geographically dispersed agreement and establishes reliable transmission.
Whether asserted teacher-disciple pedigrees can authenticate an unbroken apostolic chain.
Whether claimed apostolic lineage explains dispersed agreement and establishes reliable transmission.
Whether named teacher-disciple pedigrees authenticate an unbroken apostolic chain.
Whether historically identifiable apostles and reliable later traditions support the proposed transmission chain.
Whether later geographic agreement can be traced through well-documented apostolic identities and activity.
Whether identifiable apostles and later traditions provide a sufficiently documented chain for claims about activity and martyrdom.
Whether later geographically dispersed traditions reliably preserve knowledge about particular apostles.
Whether widespread bodily-resurrection agreement is best explained by apostolic eyewitness transmission.
Whether costly adherence by later Christians verifies the truth of the transmitted resurrection claim.
Whether widespread agreement and expansion are best explained by apostolic transmission of bodily-resurrection testimony.
Whether costly adherence to inherited teaching establishes the truth of its historical content.
Whether costly conversion and sustained proclamation require only sincere belief and ordinary movement-growth mechanisms.
Whether the costly witnesses can be connected to identifiable eyewitness testimony rather than later legend.
Whether sincerity, social benefits, and ordinary conversion mechanisms adequately explain costly early proclamation and expansion.
Whether the relevant persecuted converts and proclaimers are historically documented and connected to eyewitnesses.
Whether claimed eyewitness contact discriminates reliable transmission from rival pedigree claims.
